\chapter{Ni --- Joining Two Absences}
\label{ch:ni}
\hlchaptermodality{234}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I want neither of two things.}

I can say I want neither of two things.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ni]{ni — joining two absences}

\label{lesson:ES-C61-ni}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Y} joins two things you have. \emph{O} offers a choice between them.

Now: neither one.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{No quiero café} \emph{\textbf{ni}} \emph{agua.} — I don't want coffee or water.
\end{quote}

\textbf{ni} is Latin \emph{\textbf{nec}}, and the important thing about it is that the \emph{no} is \textbf{inside} the word. It does not mean \emph{or}; it means \emph{and not}.

So it is not the negative twin of \emph{y}. It is a word that carries its own refusal, which is why it can start a phrase on its own: \emph{\textbf{Ni}} \emph{café.} — \emph{Not even coffee.}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Look again at that sentence and count the negatives.

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{No}} \emph{quiero café} \emph{\textbf{ni}} \emph{agua.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Two} — and it is correct. English was taught to treat two negatives as cancelling out; Spanish never agreed. Here they \textbf{agree with each other} instead: the sentence is negative, so every part of it that can be negative, is.

This is worth holding on to, because it will keep happening. Once a Spanish sentence turns negative, the negativity spreads rather than doubling back.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{No quiero café ni agua}
  \item \emph{Ni café} — not even coffee
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two negatives in one Spanish sentence — right or wrong? (\textbf{Right.} They agree rather than cancel.)

And what is hiding inside \emph{ni}? (A \emph{\textbf{no}} — it means \emph{and not}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
